title: I Survived 100 Days After My Cruise Ship Sank
hook: The ship is sinking. You have one minute.
description:
At 3:17 a.m. the alarm sounds and the cruise ship starts to tilt. Milo and deck officer Rosa end up in a life raft with a dead beacon and drift for 100 days, learning real sea-survival facts: the emergency alarm, how to jump with a lifejacket, cold shock and the 1-10-1 rule, why you never drink seawater, catching rain, sharks, storms and signal mirrors.

The story is fiction; the survival facts are real. This is not professional safety training — on a real ship, follow the crew.

Next episode: 100 Days in the Desert After a Plane Crash.

Sources:
Canadian Safe Boating Council — 1-10-1 Principle https://csbc.ca/1-10-1-principle
U.S. Army — Tips to survive a fall into cold water (HELP and Huddle) https://www.army.mil/article/212474/tips_to_survive_a_fall_into_cold_water
NOAA — Why can't people drink seawater? https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/drinksw.html
SOLAS general emergency alarm (7 short + 1 long) https://ialacolreg.com/en/academy/modules/emergencies/musters-alarms?rule=alarms

shorts.title: The Alarm Every Cruise Passenger Must Know
Day 33 on a Life Raft: Sharks Arrive

scenes.say: Three seventeen a.m. Deck nine. A deep boom. Your cup slides off the table. The floor is tilting.
Then the alarm. Seven short blasts, one long. The ship is in trouble, and you're about to spend one hundred days at sea.
Milo was on holiday. Big glasses, yellow raincoat, flip flops. Now his dark cabin is leaning sideways.
Lifejacket! Put it on right now, before you leave the cabin. Do not go back for anything.
That's Rosa, a deck officer. So, can a tourist in flip flops survive one hundred days adrift? Let's see.
That alarm is real. Under the international SOLAS rules, seven short blasts and one long is the general emergency alarm.
It doesn't mean jump. It means lifejacket on, go to your muster station, and wait for the captain's orders.
Milo runs for the elevator. Rosa pulls him back. No elevators. If the power fails, you're trapped in a steel box.
This is the captain. Abandon ship. Abandon ship. Proceed to your lifeboats.
But the ship leans so far that Milo's lifeboat station is now hanging over empty air.
Rosa points down. A life raft has inflated below. We jump. The right way.
Here's how sailors are taught. Jump from as low as you can. Check below is clear. Cross your arms over your lifejacket.
Legs together. Look straight ahead, not down. Then step off and go in feet first.
Milo jumps. Three metres of falling. Then the ocean hits him like a wall of ice.
His body gasps on its own. Fast, wild breathing. This is cold shock, one of the deadliest moments of the night.
Boating experts teach the one ten one rule. About one minute to get your breathing under control. Float, and breathe slowly.
About ten minutes of useful movement before your arms stop working. Use it to reach something that floats.
And roughly one hour before the cold can make you pass out. Without his lifejacket, Milo would be under.
Rosa reaches him. Don't swim hard, it burns heat. Kick slowly. We go together.
If help isn't close, stay still. Knees up, arms hugging them. That's the HELP position. With others, you huddle to share warmth.
Rosa hauls Milo over the side of the life raft. He collapses onto the wet floor, shaking.
Behind them, the lights of the ship go out, one deck at a time.
Day two. Grey, empty sea in every direction. No ship. No lifeboats. Just an orange raft and two people.
The storm pushed them miles from the others. And the raft's emergency beacon? Cracked open. Dead.
Rosa opens the survival bag. Water pouches. Food bars. Flares. A signal mirror. A fishing kit. A bailer and a pump.
First rule. Nobody touches this water without asking. We share it. Every drop.
Day three. Milo is so thirsty he stares at the ocean. Just one sip, he thinks.
Never. NOAA, the US ocean agency, explains why. Seawater is so salty that your kidneys need more water to flush out the salt than you just drank.
Day four. The waves never stop. Milo is seasick, and every time, he loses precious water.
Look at the horizon, not the floor. Your eyes and ears need to agree.
Day five. The sun is brutal. On open water it hits you twice, from the sky and off the sea.
They hide under the canopy in the hottest hours. Move little, keep skin covered. Sweat is water you can't get back.
Day six. The water is going too fast. Rosa does the math. Ten more days. Maybe twelve.
Day eight. A dark cloud drifts over them. Then, the most beautiful sound in the world. Rain.
Don't drink the first rain. The canopy is covered in salt. Let it wash clean, then catch everything.
They spread the canopy like a funnel and fill every pouch, even the bailer. Then they drink all they can.
Day fifteen. Night. Milo sees a tiny light on the horizon. He grabs a flare.
Rosa stops him. Is it moving? Getting closer? We only have three flares. Only fire when someone can see it.
The light rises. It's not a ship. It's a star, coming up over the sea.
Day twenty one. The food bars are gone. But fish start gathering in the shade under the raft.
Rosa uses the fishing kit. Three days later, their first fish. Milo has never been so happy to eat something raw.
One rule surprises Milo. If water is short, eat less. Digesting food, especially protein, uses up water.
Day thirty three. Milo is trailing his hand in the cool water. Then something bumps the raft. Hard.
A grey fin slices past. Then another. Sharks, drawn in by the fish and the scraps they've been throwing overboard.
Hands in! Feet in! Nothing in the water!
Real raft advice. Keep hands and feet inside. And don't throw food scraps overboard, they call sharks to you.
Day forty seven. The sky turns black. Waves as tall as houses lift the raft and drop it.
Rosa throws out the sea anchor, an underwater parachute on a rope. It drags in the water and helps keep the raft from flipping.
Close the canopy. Spread your weight. Stay low, and bail. Bail like your life depends on it, because it does.
By dawn, the storm is gone. They're soaked and bruised. But the raft is still the right way up.
Day fifty two. The raft feels soft. An air tube is leaking. Rosa patches it from the repair kit and pumps it back up.
Day sixty. The hardest enemy now is inside Milo's head. He stops talking. He stops eating.
Rosa gives him jobs. Bail at sunrise. Fish at noon. Watch for ships. One knot on a rope for every day.
Survival experts say a daily routine helps people keep hope, and hope keeps people alive.
And it's been done. In World War Two, a ship's steward drifted one hundred thirty three days alone on a raft, and lived.
Day seventy four. No rain for eleven days. The last pouch is almost empty. Their lips crack.
Rosa's rule. Small sips through the day. Talk less. Stay in the shade.
Day seventy seven. Milo spots one tall cloud that isn't moving, while every other cloud drifts past.
Sailors have used this trick for centuries. A cloud that stays put at sea can mean an island underneath.
But they can't steer. The current carries them past. The cloud disappears behind them.
Day eighty. That night, the rain finally comes back.
Day eighty eight. A faint hum. A plane, high above, heading straight across the sky.
Milo fires a flare. But the plane is far too high and too fast. It doesn't turn.
Milo cries for the first time in weeks. Rosa holds out the mirror. Next time, we use this.
A signal mirror is one of the best rescue tools. On a sunny day, its flash can be seen many kilometres away.
To aim it, make a V with your other hand around the target, and tilt the mirror until the light lands inside the V.
Day ninety nine. Dawn. A dark shape on the horizon. Low, slow, getting bigger. A fishing boat.
Not the flare yet. It's sunny. Use the mirror. Aim through your fingers and keep flashing.
Flash. Flash. Flash. For twenty long minutes, nothing happens. Then the boat begins to turn.
Now the flare! Milo fires the last one. A red light over the water. The boat sounds its horn.
Fishing boat to raft. We see you. Stay where you are. We are coming to you.
Day one hundred. Hands pull them onto a solid deck. Milo's legs have forgotten how to stand.
Thinner, sunburned, salty, and very much alive.
So, could you survive one hundred days adrift? Here's what kept Milo and Rosa alive.
One. Seven short, one long: lifejacket on, go to your muster station. Two. Jump low, arms crossed, feet first.
Three. In cold water, control your breathing first, then stay still and huddle. Four. Never drink seawater.
Five. Catch rain once the salt washes off. Six. Save flares for what you can see, and flash a mirror.
Next time, Milo's plane goes down in the middle of the desert. Subscribe so you don't miss it.
